heading: 1705 — List of Company Employees (Monsterrol VOC)
html: 1705 — List of Company Employees (Monsterrol VOC)

text: The 1705 Monsterrol is a list of all Company employees at the Cape in 1705. Each employee is listed in a hierarchy which is headed by the Governor, Willem Adriaan [Adrien] Van der Stel (q.v.) which explains why the data are listed in their original sequence: namely, to preserve the status order for the user of this data. Each employee is listed with their occupation, wage scale and when they arrived. This is a document which is found in Holland and thus may be new to most researchers here. The compiler has added a column of how many slaves each owned, based on aggregation of the discrete list of slave transfers, also included on this CD. (q.v.). Click on a number to view the records or scroll through the database to appreciate the immaculate order of the Company hierarchy. Or pick up a name, and put it in the search engine, to see what happened to that person. The 1705 Monsterrol VOC database contains 542 entries

text: Translation of the E.V. Stade article by Marianne Gertenbach From: Zuid Afrika (April 1952):
html:
Translation of the E.V. Stade article
by Marianne Gertenbach
From: Zuid Afrika (April 1952):

text: The impressive map collection in the Dutch Topographic Services brought to light by C. Koeman in 1950 gives a new perspective on Dutch activities in South Africa and is being included in the publication of the Tabulae geographicae Coloniae Bonae Spei.
html: The impressive map collection in the Dutch Topographic Services brought to light by C. Koeman in 1950 gives a new perspective on Dutch activities in South Africa and is being included in the publication of the Tabulae geographicae Coloniae Bonae Spei.

text: It also contains a series of six drawings described in Mr. Koeman’s inventory in the Tijdskrif van het Koninklijk Nederlandsch Aardrijkskundig Genootschap, volume LXIX, no.1, under 293 as follows:
html: It also contains a series of six drawings described in Mr. Koeman’s inventory in the Tijdskrif van het Koninklijk Nederlandsch Aardrijkskundig Genootschap, volume LXIX, no.1, under 293 as follows:

text: 293 a Drawing of the Colony of Stellenbosch … miles from the Castle of the Cape of Good Hope, 15 February 1710. O,40 x,30. . .Signed: E.V. Stade.
html: 293 a Drawing of the Colony of Stellenbosch … miles from the Castle of the Cape of Good Hope, 15 February 1710. O,40 x,30. . .Signed: E.V. Stade.

text: Cape of Good Hope 1710. 0,40 x 0,30: Signed E.V. Stade.

html: Constantia, the estate of Simon van der Stel, 31 January 1710. 0,40 x 0,30. Signed by E.V.Stade.

text: Drakenstein colony at the Cape of Good Hope where the church is, situated about … hours from the Castle, March 1710. 0,30 x,30. Signed E.V. Stade.
html: Drakenstein colony at the Cape of Good Hope where the church is, situated about … hours from the Castle, March 1710. 0,30 x,30. Signed E.V. Stade.

text: These drawings by E.V. Stade are amongst the earliest of the Cape. Only a few series of pictures of the Cape from the 18th century exist: the sketches that Col. Robert Jacob Gordon made while travelling with Gov. van Plettenberg in 1749, the drawings by Johannes Schumacher on his travels with Hendrik Swellengrebel 1776, Johannes Rach’s drawings of the Cape in 1764, five views of the Cape by J.W. Heydt in his publication on the East Indies in 1741 and a watercolour of Table Mountain from the bay, 1655-6.
html: These drawings by E.V. Stade are amongst the earliest of the Cape. Only a few series of pictures of the Cape from the 18th century exist: the sketches that Col. Robert Jacob Gordon made while travelling with Gov. van Plettenberg in 1749, the drawings by Johannes Schumacher on his travels with Hendrik Swellengrebel 1776, Johannes Rach’s drawings of the Cape in 1764, five views of the Cape by J.W. Heydt in his publication on the East Indies in 1741 and a watercolour of Table Mountain from the bay, 1655-6.

text: E.V. Stade’s drawings of 1710 show the settlement at the Castle – seen from the bay and from the mountain - as well as four scenes inland : Constantia, Stellenbosch, Drakenstein and Paarl. Of particular importance is the view of Stellenbosch, the earliest known, with the original church intact – it was burnt down later that year and this, to my knowledge, is the only picture of it. The drawings are dated and were made between 25 January and sometime in March 1710.
html: E.V. Stade’s drawings of 1710 show the settlement at the Castle – seen from the bay and from the mountain - as well as four scenes inland : Constantia, Stellenbosch, Drakenstein and Paarl. Of particular importance is the view of Stellenbosch, the earliest known, with the original church intact – it was burnt down later that year and this, to my knowledge, is the only picture of it. The drawings are dated and were made between 25 January and sometime in March 1710.

text: Who was the artist, E.V. Stade? He is not listed amongst the residents at the Cape in 1710 nor should he be confused with Marten van Staden and Willem van Staden from Haarlem both living in Drakenstein — although they may have been related, an "n" here or there meant little in those days.
html: Who was the artist, E.V. Stade? He is not listed amongst the residents at the Cape in 1710 nor should he be confused with Marten van Staden and Willem van Staden from Haarlem both living in Drakenstein — although they may have been related, an "n" here or there meant little in those days.

text: It is more likely that the artist arrived with the return fleet that was in Table Bay between the 10 January and 2 April, the crew having boarded the ship by the 28 March. The VOC ship-lists relate to ships leaving the Netherlands but not return fleets and only senior personnel are listed. E.V. Stade doesn’t appear amongst any of them.

The VOC ship-lists relate to ships leaving the Netherlands but not return fleets and only senior personnel are listed. E.V. Stade doesn’t appear amongst any of them.

text: However, the admiral of the return fleet at the Cape in 1700 — Joan van Hoorn was married to a grand-daughter of Jan van Riebeeck and her letters have been published by D.B Bosman, Briewe van Johanna van Riebeeck en ander Riebeeckiana. Johanna Maria’s father, Abraham van Riebeeck, was Governor General of the Dutch East Indies 1709–13. Her husband, Joan van Hoorn was almost twice her age — he 57 and she 30; Johanna Maria was his third wife but she herself was widowed and married again after his death. The Van Riebeeck name died out with a nephew of hers, leaving only descendants on the female line.

Johanna Maria’s father, Abraham van Riebeeck, was Governor General of the Dutch East Indies 1709–13. Her husband, Joan van Hoorn was almost twice her age — he 57 and she 30; Johanna Maria was his third wife but she herself was widowed and married again after his death. The Van Riebeeck name died out with a nephew of hers, leaving only descendants on the female line.

text: Johanna Maria and her husband wrote from the Cape to her parents in Batavia. Abraham van Riebeeck stopped over at the Cape in 1676 and was favourably impressed. The negative reports that he now received from his daughter and son-in-law were disturbing. Jan van Hoorn found the castle, the heads, the drains, the stores and watch houses in a bad state of repair and sections of walls plastered only with mud not the proper lime mixture. Governor van Assenburgh [who took over in 1708] described the Cape as suffering from an overdose of eating and drinking. Johanna Maria accused him of consorting with the worst sort of women and went on to give further descriptions of the miserable conditions and degeneracy of the people at the Cape ...

The negative reports that he now received from his daughter and son-in-law were disturbing. Jan van Hoorn found the castle, the heads, the drains, the stores and watch houses in a bad state of repair and sections of walls plastered only with mud not the proper lime mixture. Governor van Assenburgh [who took over in 1708] described the Cape as suffering from an overdose of eating and drinking. Johanna Maria accused him of consorting with the worst sort of women and went on to give further descriptions of the miserable conditions and degeneracy of the people at the Cape ...

text: Apparently the van Hoorns did not venture far from the Castle where they stayed and describe the officials and burghers they met there, commenting on the impact of the conflict with the former Governor WA van der Stel. They visited former Governor Simon van der Stel at Constantia, and were aware of Govert Knol’s visit to the warm baths at Caledon.

They visited former Governor Simon van der Stel at Constantia, and were aware of Govert Knol’s visit to the warm baths at Caledon.

text: There is a possibility that Abraham van Riebeeck, the Governor General, who was born at the Cape in 1653 had commissioned Van Stade’s drawings as a souvenir of his early childhood here. In a postscript to her letter of 16 March 1710 Johanna Maria van Riebeeck writes: "PS : Sending herewith on the Amazone the pictures of the Cape, which in my opinion are a good likeness . The artist is most of the time sick."

In a postscript to her letter of 16 March 1710 Johanna Maria van Riebeeck writes: "PS : Sending herewith on the Amazone the pictures of the Cape, which in my opinion are a good likeness . The artist is most of the time sick."

text: Were Stade’s drawings preliminary sketches for a completed picture sent to Batavia? According to Prof Bosman, who had contact with the descendants, no such picture is in the family’s possession. The Stade pictures that remained at the Cape became part of the Van der Graaff collection, brought to the Netherlands at the end of 18th century.

According to Prof Bosman, who had contact with the descendants, no such picture is in the family’s possession. The Stade pictures that remained at the Cape became part of the Van der Graaff collection, brought to the Netherlands at the end of 18th century.

text: If the sketches were done locally, surely a sick man would have been noticed on his trips to the outlying districts, Paarl, Stellenbosch & Drakenstein. Could Stade have arrived as a sick man on the return fleet or was he already at the Cape convalescing in the hospital?
html: If the sketches were done locally, surely a sick man would have been noticed on his trips to the outlying districts, Paarl, Stellenbosch & Drakenstein. Could Stade have arrived as a sick man on the return fleet or was he already at the Cape convalescing in the hospital?

text: When did he do the picture of Constantia? At the left of the picture one gets a glimpse of False Bay and a ship in full sail, annotated the Abbekerk. The drawing is dated 31 January but the ship only arrived at the Cape on 4 February. The Abbekerk, equipped by the Chamber of Hoorn, left Texel on 10 June 1709 and arrived at the Cape on 4 February 1710. She sailed on the 2 April and arrived in Batavia on 4 July 1710. In March Johanna Maria van Riebeeck wrote to her parents that she would be sending them preserved vegetables with that ship.
html: When did he do the picture of Constantia? At the left of the picture one gets a glimpse of False Bay and a ship in full sail, annotated the Abbekerk. The drawing is dated 31 January but the ship only arrived at the Cape on 4 February. The Abbekerk, equipped by the Chamber of Hoorn, left Texel on 10 June 1709 and arrived at the Cape on 4 February 1710. She sailed on the 2 April and arrived in Batavia on 4 July 1710. In March Johanna Maria van Riebeeck wrote to her parents that she would be sending them preserved vegetables with that ship.

text: As Stade was already at the Cape in January 1710 he could not have arrived with the Abbekerk but might have left with it for Batavia. However, his name does not appear in the files of the Landsargief at Djakarta, nor in the Museum of the Bataviaasch Genootschap, nor in the Prentekabinet in Amsterdam. We are no closer to discovering who the artist is, but can only reflect on his work.

text: Stade seemed more interested in focussing on details rather than in general landscapes and views. He seems to be looking down on the objects and wandering through the terrain, depicting the houses, alleys and neatly placed trees, but not from any particular angle. He loses proportion, making houses too high e.g. his picture of Cape Town and of Constantia (the only picture of the farm at that time). There are odd features such as a curved bridge close to the Castle which is made to look like ones in Amsterdam with a round opening for the flow of water. In the two pictures of Cape Town discrepancies in the layout of the houses and streets cast doubt on the reliability of his observations.
html: Stade seemed more interested in focussing on details rather than in general landscapes and views. He seems to be looking down on the objects and wandering through the terrain, depicting the houses, alleys and neatly placed trees, but not from any particular angle. He loses proportion, making houses too high e.g. his picture of Cape Town and of Constantia (the only picture of the farm at that time). There are odd features such as a curved bridge close to the Castle which is made to look like ones in Amsterdam with a round opening for the flow of water. In the two pictures of Cape Town discrepancies in the layout of the houses and streets cast doubt on the reliability of his observations.

text: The two pictures reproduced here show the Castle and Stellenbosch. The picture of Stellenbosch has only recently come to light. How quaint the town looks with Dutch gables on the houses and the enclosed farmyards. The church has no windows - was this an accidental omission? In the following article, a colleague discusses the accuracy of this picture. Hopefully the same will be done for the pictures of Drakenstein and Paarl.

text: As an old Stellenboscher I would like to add some comments about the picture Van Stade made in 1710, by far the oldest picture of Stellenbosch. It shows a small and primitive settlement surrounded by the large expanse of nature.
html: As an old Stellenboscher I would like to add some comments about the picture Van Stade made in 1710, by far the oldest picture of Stellenbosch. It shows a small and primitive settlement surrounded by the large expanse of nature.

text: The representation of the comb of Botmanskop, precisely behind the town, is true to nature. The other mountains, not quite as successfully depicted, appear in their correct positions and as a whole the profile of the mountains is recognisable. Our artist had a feel for the topography of the landscape.
html: The representation of the comb of Botmanskop, precisely behind the town, is true to nature. The other mountains, not quite as successfully depicted, appear in their correct positions and as a whole the profile of the mountains is recognisable. Our artist had a feel for the topography of the landscape.

text: The veld looks bare and tame — more so than it would have been despite the clearing of bush in 1679 and lacks wild animals.
html: The veld looks bare and tame — more so than it would have been despite the clearing of bush in 1679 and lacks wild animals.

text: The picture corresponds with information given by Francois Valentijn in the year 1705 that the town consisted of 13-14 houses. All the houses had one or more outbuildings and therefore the settlement looks bigger than it was. The boundary of the town land was the Eerste River, which runs from the mountains and can be seen on the right. Dorp Street is wider and without its famous oaks which writers refer to during the 18th century. The most important building is the Drostdy burnt down in 1762 with its pointed roof: together with adjacent buildings it stands on the site of the present day seminary.

text: Opposite is Drostdy Street running west and showing the original Church which was burnt down with the whole town in December 1710: only a couple of houses were spared. According to pictures in the Swellengrebel collection, the church was rebuilt on the left of Drostdy Street. Changes to Dorp Street after the fire in 1762 are not obvious in the drawing. Shown in both pictures of 1710 and 1757 is a small free-standing house, on the corner, diagonally opposite the Drostdy: this is the site of one of the oldest and coldest building in town. The pyramid shape structure in Dorp Street standing on an open field opposite the site of the old gaol, must be the gallows.

text: The farm on a rise at the end of the town is either that of Mr Marais at the entrance to Jonkershoek or Schoongezicht of Adjutant Izak Schrijver, well known for his journal — the other farms with their ring walls are not so easily distinguished.
